opus-5.5.text:
I think tool use is one of the most exciting frontiers for robotics right now, because it changes how we think about what a robot *is*.

Traditionally, a robot's capabilities were defined by its hardware: what the gripper can grasp, how far the arm can reach, how much force the motors can produce. Tool use breaks that ceiling. Humans aren't especially strong or fast, but we pick up a hammer, a knife, or a lever and suddenly we can do things our bodies alone never could. I think robots can follow the same path. If a robot can understand and use tools, its effective capability set is no longer fixed at design time. It grows with the environment around it.

I see it at two levels. The first is physical tool use: picking up a spatula, using a screwdriver, pushing an object with a stick to reach something farther away. This is very hard, because the robot has to reason about the robot plus the tool as a new combined body. Contact dynamics, force transmission, how the tool slips in the hand. These are hard to hand-engineer, and that's where learning, simulation, and large-scale data really help.

The second level, which I find just as important, is what we might call digital tool use, the way large language models call APIs, search, run code, or query other models. When you combine a foundation model's reasoning with robot embodiment, the robot can decide: "To finish this task, I need to look something up," or "I should call a perception module," or "I should write a small program to plan this motion." The robot becomes an agent that orchestrates many capabilities, not a single monolithic policy.

What ties them together is generalization. The real goal isn't teaching a robot to use one specific hammer. It's for the robot to see an object it has never seen and ask: what can I do with this? Could this serve as a tool for my goal? That's the kind of common-sense, physically grounded reasoning that I think vision-language-action models are starting to make possible. We're still early. Dexterity, reliability, and safety are all real challenges. But I believe tool use is a key step from robots that execute pre-programmed skills toward robots that are genuinely general-purpose physical agents.

r002.rationale: The response mentions search and looking things up as digital tools, but does not explain that web search provides knowledge beyond what is encoded in the underlying model.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think tool use is one of the most underappreciated levers we have in robotics right now, and the way I like to frame it is this: a robot's body is fixed, but its capabilities don't have to be.

When we design a robot, we make a lot of hard commitments. The gripper has a certain width, the arm has a certain reach, the force it can apply is bounded by its motors. Historically, if you wanted a robot to do something outside that envelope, you redesigned the hardware. That's slow and expensive. Tool use breaks that constraint. A robot that can pick up a stick suddenly has longer reach. A robot that can use a spatula can manipulate things it could never grasp directly. A screwdriver turns a general-purpose hand into a precision instrument. So in one sense, tools are how a physical agent extends its own morphology on demand, the same way humans do.

But I think the deeper point is about what tool use reveals about intelligence. Using a tool well requires the robot to understand the affordances of an object that isn't part of its body, reason about how that object changes the physics of the interaction, and adapt its control in real time. If you grab a hammer, your dynamics change. The center of mass shifts, the contact point moves out to the head of the hammer, and you have to swing differently. A robot that can do this has to have some internal model of itself plus the tool as a combined system. That's a much richer kind of embodied reasoning than just reaching and grasping.

What's exciting to me is that the foundation model wave is making this tractable in a way it wasn't five years ago. Large vision-language models already know what a hammer is for, what a ladle does, how a wrench fits a bolt. That semantic knowledge about tools is baked in from internet-scale data. The gap has been connecting that knowledge to actual low-level control, and that's where I've spent a lot of my career, on sim-to-real, on learning locomotion and manipulation policies that actually run on hardware. When you bring those two together, you get a robot that can look at a new object, infer it might be useful as a tool, and figure out how to use it, instead of being limited to a fixed library of behaviors.

I'd also say tool use is where generalization gets tested honestly. It's easy to overfit a policy to one object. It's much harder to learn a representation of "pushing" or "scooping" or "prying" that transfers across different tools of different shapes. If we get that right, we're not just adding one more skill, we're multiplying the robot's effective skill set by every object in the environment. That's the leap from a robot that does tasks to a robot that solves problems.

And I'll admit, the simulation side still matters enormously here. Tool interactions involve contact-rich dynamics that are hard to model, and rare in real-world data. Being able to simulate thousands of variations of a robot using a tool, then transfer that to the physical system, is how we're going to scale this without breaking a lot of hardware along the way.

astra-6.text:
I think tool use is a very powerful way to expand what a robot can do. A robot’s body gives it certain capabilities, but those capabilities don’t have to be fixed. A gripper alone cannot do everything, but if it can pick up a screwdriver, a brush, or a pair of scissors, suddenly it can perform a much wider range of tasks without changing its hardware.

The interesting challenge is that using a tool changes how the robot interacts with the world. If you’re holding a hammer, you need to reason about where the head of the hammer is, how it moves, and how much force to apply. It’s not enough to recognize the tool or know what it’s for. You need the physical skill to use it, and you need feedback to know whether it’s working.

So I see tool use as a bridge between high-level reasoning and physical intelligence. The robot needs to decide, ‘What tool would help me accomplish this goal?’ Then it needs to execute that decision in the real world. If we can make that process general enough that a robot can learn to use unfamiliar tools, we can expand its capabilities far beyond the tasks we explicitly trained it to perform.

sol-6.1.text:
I think tool use changes what it means for a robot to have a capability. The robot doesn’t have to build every capability into its own body. A gripper alone may not be able to turn a screw, but if it can pick up and use a screwdriver, suddenly that task becomes possible. It can extend its reach, apply more force, or interact with objects more precisely by choosing the right tool.

But the interesting part is that using a tool requires more than recognizing it. The robot has to understand how to grasp it, how its motion translates into an effect at the other end, and whether that effect is actually happening. When you hold a hammer, for example, you’re controlling the hammerhead through your hand. A robot needs to make that same connection through perception, action, and feedback.

So I see tool use as a way to move beyond a fixed set of trained behaviors. We want a robot that can encounter a new task, identify a useful tool, and figure out how to use it. That ability to combine what it already knows with what’s available in the environment could make robots much more adaptable.
